title: pkix-lint: an expect() whose safety rests on two predicates staying in sync
description:
## What

`Rfc8398SmimeMailboxEquivalenceLint::check_cert` (rfc8398.rs:352 and the
matching loop below it) calls

    mailbox_equivalent(r, u).expect("pre-validation ensures inputs are well-formed")

inside a cross-match loop. The panic is unreachable today, and the
argument for that is spread across two functions with a comment holding
them together.

## Why it is safe now

Verified 2026-11-27 by reading both predicates:

`validate_mailbox_for_equivalence` (rfc8398.rs:388) rejects
  - no '@' delimiter
  - empty local-part
  - empty domain
  - a domain `idna::domain_to_ascii` will not convert

`mailbox_equivalent` (rfc8398.rs:418) can only return `Err` for
  - either side having no '@'
  - either side having an empty local-part or domain
  - the smtputf8 domain failing A-label conversion

The first set covers the second exactly, and `check_cert` runs the
validator over both collections before the loops. So the `expect` holds.

## Why it is still worth changing

This crate's contract is that a lint reports findings and does not
panic -- it is run over attacker-supplied certificates. The invariant
that makes the `expect` sound is not expressed in any type or asserted by
any test; it is a comment saying "pre-validation above guarantees".
Anyone adding an error case to `mailbox_equivalent` -- a length cap, a
forbidden-character check, a stricter IDN profile -- turns a lint finding
into a process abort, and nothing fails first to tell them.

AGENTS.md's error-handling guidance is that a panic belongs where
reaching it means in-process code broke an obligation. That is the case
here, so the `expect` is not wrong. The gap is that the obligation is
undocumented in the only places a change would be made.

## Options

1. A validated newtype -- `ValidatedMailbox<'a>` produced by
   `validate_mailbox_for_equivalence` and consumed by
   `mailbox_equivalent`, so the pre-validation is carried in the type and
   the function cannot be called without it. Removes the `expect`
   entirely. Most work, most durable.
2. A test asserting the two predicates agree: for a table of malformed
   inputs, every one `mailbox_equivalent` errors on is one
   `validate_mailbox_for_equivalence` also rejects. Cheap, and it fails
   the moment someone widens either side.
3. Leave it and expand the comment at both functions to say the coupling
   exists and in which direction. Cheapest, least durable.

Option 2 is probably the right ratio -- it is a dozen lines and it
actually breaks when the invariant does, which the comment cannot.

## Found by

The pkix-lint mutation sweep, 2026-11-27, which took that crate from 104
survivors to 8. Not one of them -- no mutation reaches the panic, because
no mutation makes the validator weaker. It surfaced from reading the two
functions together.
